name: wayland
desc: Protocol for a compositor to talk to its clients
why: The Wayland protocol is a real door into how display servers talk to clients, though the formula is mostly libraries and the famous name lowers its surprise.

brief.what_it_is: Wayland is a protocol and system architecture for graphical display, meant to replace the X11 window system protocol. Applications (clients) use the Wayland protocol to talk to a display server (a compositor) to make themselves visible and to receive user input. The page describes it as a language rather than a single program: there is no common Wayland server like Xorg, and each graphical environment ships its own compositor implementation. The core library, libwayland, translates protocol definitions written in XML into a C API, and it only encodes and decodes messages.
brief.why_it_exists: The page says Wayland is a replacement for the X11 window system protocol and architecture, aimed at being easier to develop, extend, and maintain.
brief.how_it_works: Protocol definitions are written in XML, and libwayland converts them into a C language API for encoding and decoding messages between compositor and clients. The compositor and the applications are separate processes that talk over that protocol. Window management and user experience are often tied to the compositor rather than swappable parts.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no installation steps, accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration. The formula's listed executable is wayland-scanner, which the homepage does not mention.
brief.standout: Unlike X11, there is no single canonical server: the protocol is the shared contract, and every desktop environment brings its own compositor. The page also notes Wayland can run nested inside another X11 or Wayland session, and that some web browsers use it for internal communication between application parts.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows no release date, last commit, or maintenance note. It does list releases, git repositories, a mailing list, IRC channel #wayland on OFTC, and a bug tracker, which suggests an active project, but I did not verify recency.
brief.caveats: The formula is a library and protocol toolkit, not a standalone application, so installing it gives you little to run directly. The page says libwayland 'does not implement Wayland'; the real behaviour lives in compositors and toolkits. The homepage has no platform or licensing details.
quotes: Wayland is a replacement for the X11 window system protocol and architecture with the aim to be easier to develop, extend, and maintain.

judge.reason: Wayland is well known, but its protocol-first design—where each desktop supplies its own compositor—makes a genuinely interesting system to explore.

entry.title: Wayland
entry.tldr: The protocol that replaces X11 for talking to a display server, with wayland-scanner turning its XML protocol definitions into C code.
entry.deeper_look:
Wayland is a protocol and architecture for putting graphics on a screen. Applications are clients, and a display server called a compositor draws their windows and passes along keyboard and mouse input. The homepage describes it as a language rather than a program: "Wayland is the language (protocol) that applications can use to talk to a display server in order to make themselves visible and get input from the user (a person)."

The idea underneath is that the protocol is the shared contract. Unlike X11, there is no single canonical server. In the project's words, "every graphical environment brings with it one of many compositor implementations." Window management and much of the user experience tend to live in the compositor instead of in swappable parts.

The protocols themselves are written in XML. The core library, libwayland, turns those definitions into a C API that only encodes and decodes messages between compositor and clients. It does not implement Wayland. The page says Wayland can also run nested inside another X11 or Wayland session, and that some web browsers use it for internal communication between their own parts.

The one executable this formula installs is wayland-scanner. The brief does not describe it, so treat it as the tool that works with those XML definitions, and read its help output to see what it offers.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the scanner's usage, a first look at the tool that works with Wayland's XML protocol definitions.

entry.whats_unique: It is a protocol with no reference server: every desktop brings its own compositor, and the XML definitions are the thing everyone agrees on.
entry.caveats: The formula is a library and protocol toolkit, not an application, so there is little to run directly; the real behaviour lives in compositors, and the brief could not confirm project recency.
